A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same graph-based amortized Bayesian inference work. All 25 pages of v3 and 31 pages of v5, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original simulation results for fixed- and variable-size toy graphs, mouse microbiome transmission, and train scheduling, including architecture comparisons and calibration analyses.

after.justification: v5 retains those original results and adds observed mouse-data inference, predictive checks, training-size experiments, and a simplified-toy comparison against MCMC.

M1.justification: The encoder–posterior-estimator pipeline, architectures, pooling mechanisms, and training objectives remain unchanged. The new experiments configure existing components; flow matching, used for the observed mouse data, was already described and tested in v3.

E1.justification: v3's biological evaluation uses a simulator motivated by mouse observations. v5 Section 3.3 actually analyzes observed data comprising 177 mice and 52 microbial taxa, substantially extending evaluation beyond simulations. Appendix C also adds a tractable toy scenario without triadic closure; the original scenarios remain.

E2.justification: Appendix C adds HMC implemented in Stan as a comparator to Set Transformer/PMA-based ABI on the simplified toy model. This addition is confined to that comparison; the original Deep Sets, GCN, Graph Transformer, and Set Transformer comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce substantial protocols: fixed observed mouse topology with only the exchange factor inferred, 10,000 offline training simulations, training-size sweeps from 3,200 to 32,000 datasets, and a simplified-toy comparison using 500 test graphs. Graph-statistic calibration and Jaccard-based predictive checks add evaluation quantities and procedures. The original experiments' settings are retained.

E4.justification: v5 adds training-size sensitivity analysis in Appendix A, calibration checks using four graph statistics in Appendix B, and observed-mouse prior/posterior predictive checks in Section 3.3. These examine data requirements, structural fidelity, and simulator misspecification beyond v3's retained pooling, graph-size, and observation-horizon analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix C newly specifies four HMC chains per test graph, and calibration assessment expands to data-dependent quantities. The existing five-run medians, minimum–maximum error bars, and 95% intervals are retained; no increase in runs for the original experiments is stated.

E6.justification: Original numerical tables and plotted results are retained, including v3 Table 3 becoming v5 Table 4. Added results include the observed-mouse exchange-factor posterior mean of 0.144 and standard deviation of 0.009, predictive mismatch, training-size/runtime findings, and structural calibration failures. On the new simplified toy model, ABI–MCMC posterior-median correlations are 0.996, 0.994, and 0.999, while ABI shows poorer log-likelihood calibration.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds mathematical definitions for newly evaluated graph quantities: spectral gap, edge density, degree assortativity, and transitivity. This is a limited definitional addition; the original ABI, architecture, and parameter-calibration equations remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The introduction qualifies the research gap by acknowledging prior spatial and problem-specific graph inference, positioning the missing contribution as a general graph-ABI framework. The abstract's central contribution and the summary's recommendation of Set Transformer with attention pooling remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 newly identifies simulator misspecification as the principal explanation for the observed-mouse predictive mismatch and explicitly leaves that biological modeling gap unresolved. Appendix B extends the high-recovery explanation to data-level calibration failures, while Appendix C interprets agreement with MCMC and the remaining log-likelihood calibration discrepancy. These materially expand the applicability boundaries and interpretation.

D1.justification: v5 adds observed-data construction and taxon-filtering instructions, new training budgets, BayesFlow/Stan implementation information, and CPU, RAM, and runtime reporting. Section 2.4 also newly clarifies that evaluation metrics use unseen simulated test data. The existing code-access disclosure is retained; removing '.git' from its URL does not change availability.

R1.justification: The introduction adds Sainsbury-Dale et al. and Stillman et al. as relevant graph-inference precedents. Additional references support SBI evaluation, biological network analysis, graph statistics, and HMC. These provide targeted positioning and methodological context without substantially restructuring the literature discussion.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains intact. Changes include local grammar and terminology corrections, additional cross-references, insertion of the observed-data section and new appendices, and corresponding renumbering. The original mice appendix is moved from B to D rather than removed.

P2.justification: v5 substantially expands the visual evidence with observed-data posterior and predictive-check plots, training-size curves, structural-calibration panels, MCMC comparison plots, and a runtime table. Existing figure content is retained; train Figures 7–8 become Figures 9–10, and the mice results table moves to Appendix D. Publication headers and local page layouts also change.

improvement.justification: The observed-data analysis, predictive checks, and HMC/runtime comparisons provide evidence missing from v3 and expose practical limitations. These improve assessability, but the gains are qualified: Appendix B dismisses negative calibration scores despite Section 2.4 defining them as evidence of miscalibration, and the unchanged summary says all graphs have fewer than 50 nodes despite the new 177-mouse analysis. The net improvement is therefore limited.
